speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to extend to you as well as the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and all the members of the house the cordial salutations of the people of the constituency of Richelieu-Vercheres.
At the beginning of this twenty-second parliament, I wish to draw attention to the fact that the electors of Richelieu-Vercheres have been electing Liberal members for the past 12 parliaments.
I also wish to congratulate the Prime Minister on his great victory. I also want to thank him for stopping at Sorel to make a speech during the last electoral campaign.
I thank the electors of Richelieu-Vercheres for the magnificent majority they have given me, but I know such a large majority was due to the prestige of the Prime Minister and to his platform.
Mr. Speaker, may I also congratulate you on your appointment. It is an honour which is reflected not only on you but also on the whole French-Canadian people and I think it is another fine example that we may set our French-Canadian youth in order to make them understand that they have the right and the privilege of being free to attain the highest positions in the public administration of our country.
The Address-Mr. Cardin
I also wish to congratulate the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Lesage) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) who have become members of the cabinet. These promotions were no surprise to those who knew them and I am sure that they will do a lot of good work for their country.
May I also be permitted to congratulate those numerous members who have been appointed parliamentary assistants and, while wishing them good luck in the fulfilment of their duties, I think it might be fitting to wish them patience, for I am told that members seeking a solution to some of their problems follow them through the halls and even to their homes. Well, I rest assured that these parliamentary assistants will be able to help their colleagues, being very well aware of the difficulties which they have to face.
Finally, I extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Hollingworth) and the seconder (Mr. Villeneuve) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne and together with my fellow members I wish them good luck in the career they have taken up and in which they have made such a good start.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, I was among the many thousands of Canadians who participated in Her Majesty's coronation through the medium of television. I must say that I was greatly impressed at the solemnity and splendour of that ceremony. I do not believe I was the only person who was deeply moved when our young Queen in accepting the crown accepted as well the tremendous responsibilities that have fallen upon her shoulders.
I dare say that coronation day was a great day for Great Britain and for the commonwealth nations, but it was even more than that for Canada. It was an historical moment, because for the first time in our history her gracious majesty was crowned Queen of Canada. As I watched the ceremony I could not help noticing that the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) was placed next to the Prime Minister of England in order of precedence.
This fact made me realize that Canada had not only reached adulthood but that she was now playing an extremely important part in the affairs of the commonwealth nations as well as those of the world generally. I began to wonder how in such a short time Canada had become so important, and I came to the conclusion that one of the reasons

The Address-Mr. Cardin Canada had achieved what she had was the national unity we have acquired in this country during the past 50 years.
I believe honestly and sincerely that that national unity is the greatest political achievement this country has known for a long time. I believe that national unity is the only political formula that can guarantee a brilliant future for Canada. I believe that national unity is the basic principle of our constitution. I believe that national unity is not incompatible with provincial autonomy. I have at heart the welfare of my French-Canadian compatriots as well as the welfare of my country and I am tired of hearing petty and fallacious arguments that may well undermine our national unity.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I have decided to answer as best I can any arguments that may have the effect of destroying this basic principle of our democracy. Also, Mr. Speaker, since the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) seems on many occasions to have not only the ear but the voice of the premier of Quebec, as well as that of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) I have decided to concentrate my few remarks on the speech made by that hon. member in this house not so long ago. I certainly regret that he is not in his seat now. As a matter of fact I find it far easier to speak about or accuse someone when he is in front of me rather than when he is absent. However, as you know, we cannot always control the hour at which we are going to speak.
Many hon. members may have been surprised that the hon. member for Three Rivers asked the federal government to build a bridge between Three Rivers and Ste. Angele. I cannot say that I was surprised because, during the last federal election, I heard the hon. member make the promise that the bridge would be built. However, I must say that I marvelled at his calmness and coolness and the matter of fact tone in which he made the demand. The hon. member had just finished accusing the federal government of sticking its nose into provincial affairs and of not respecting provincial autonomy. In the very next breath he went on to demand that the federal government build a bridge between two points in the province of Quebec. As everyone knows, that is one of the matters which are strictly and absolutely within provincial jurisdiction.
I do not disagree that the bridge is necessary or that it is a good thing for the economy of the province. I agree with the hon. member on those points, but I disagree with him in that being so sensitive about provincial


autonomy, he baldly demands in this house that this government should build a bridge between two points in the province of Quebec. This attitude of being neither one nor the other, neither fish nor flesh, creates a great deal of confusion not only in this house but in the country. It is something which I think should stop before we have more serious results. Also, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the hon. member for Three Rivers ask the premier of Quebec to build the bridge, seeing that he has his ear. That would be an excellent thing.
The hon. member also suggests that if the government cannot build the bridge alone it should reach some understanding with the provincial government and with the municipalities for the construction of that bridge. I believe this government has had some experience in the building of bridges in cooperation with the province of Quebec, and I am led to believe that it has not been as successful as one might have wished. As a matter of fact the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) on May 5, 1953, when making a statement regarding the abolition of tolls on the Jacques Cartier bridge in Montreal, had this to say:
Beginning in 1944, the city of Montreal and also the province of Quebec stopped making their annual contributions towards the deficit of the bridge, and it was decided to take court action against the city. Finally, on December 9, 1952, the Supreme Court of Canada maintained the decision of the Quebec court of queen's bench and of the superior court of Quebec that the city of Montreal was liable to the full extent specified by the tripartite agreement. Subsequently the city of Montreal has made payment in full of its arrears to the national harbours board in the amount of $954,833. The province of Quebec so far has not made good its arrears in the same amount.
I do not believe there is any further comment to be added to what I have already read here, Mr. Speaker, but it does not seem logical and it would not be logical for the federal government to enter into a new agreement when a previous agreement has not been fulfilled.
As you perhaps know, Mr. Speaker, there are many demands made by members of this house, by my constituents, and by many of the constituents around Montreal for abolition of the tolls on the Jacques Cartier bridge. I rather imagine that the situation which exists between the provincial and federal governments may well be one of the reasons the tolls on that particular bridge have not yet been abolished. I do hope, however, that the government will at least give consideration to the abolition of tolls on the Jacques Cartier bridge before'they consider

any other agreement with or without the province of Quebec for the construction of a bridge at Three Rivers.
The hon. member for Three Rivers in his speech claims that the federal government, contrary to our constitution, has invaded the provincial tax field to the extent that it now receives 77 per cent of the tax dollar. That is a statement I have heard many times in the house and during the recent election campaign. Well, Mr. Speaker, I submit that is not a true picture of the situation because it does not include revenues that are received from provincial sources. As a matter of fact, in 1951-52, from sources which were strictly provincial, the provinces received $493 million. In 1952-53 the amount was slightly higher. Those figures, of course, do not take into account revenues received by municipalities through municipal taxes and so on. If we were to take all the figures and group them together I am sure that the result would not be quite as great as 77 per cent and the picture would not be so black as the hon. member has painted it.
The hon. member states that Quebec is in a very precarious financial position; that it has not the finances to undertake projects that are of a purely provincial nature; that the constituencies and municipalities have not the money to take advantage of the changes that are to be made in the Bank Act and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation when municipalities will be called upon to furnish finances for public services. He painted a very black picture of the province of Quebec with respect to its financial position. It was very stirring indeed to hear him, but what he said was not quite accurate because if you recall, early last spring the minister of finance of the province of Quebec estimated that the surplus of revenue over ordinary expenditure for 1953 would be over $40 million. Since 1946 the province of Quebec has had a surplus of over $293,447,000. As you may know, Mr. Speaker, that of course does not include any of the subsidies the federal government pays to the nine other provinces of Canada. Those are sources of revenue that the province of Quebec has been able to obtain in its own domain.
The hon. member also claims that it is an easy thing for Ottawa to go ahead and to give subsidies to the different provinces because they have the money, and that Quebec would like nothing better than to be able to give subsidies to those in the province of Quebec who may need them. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that in the words of the minister of finance of Quebec himself, the province is absolutely capable of giving out subsidies.
The Address-Mr. Cardin I would suggest that they might perhaps give subsidies to the different municipalities in Quebec.
It appears to me, Mr. Speaker, that the perception of taxes as it exists in the federal government is not illegal today, as the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) claims. I believe that it is in complete accord with our constitution which allows, permits and empowers the federal government to levy taxes by any means for matters of national interest. Besides that, I believe that the responsibilities of the federal government cannot be restricted by simply restricting these powers of levying taxes. On the contrary, the responsibilities of the federal government-responsibilities that occur either by circumstances or by the will of the people- are the very factors that decide what taxes have to be levied in this country. There is not a serious Canadian who does not realize the increasing responsibilities that are being imposed upon the federal government. Even the hon. member for Three Rivers in his speech also exhorted the federal government to add a national health program to the already heavy list of responsibilities that fall on the shoulders of the federal government. Mr. Speaker, there can be no other way. Either we have responsibilities and we give the people what they want or we do not; either we face 'our obligations and we tax, or we do not. If we do not, then to my mind it is the beginning of the end.
The hon. member speaks of the redistribution of taxes. That is all very well. It makes very good speech material, but it always ends up in the same way. Last year we had a budget of $4J billion. Of that, $2J billion went for defence, $1 billion went for social legislation and $1 billion went for administration and for reduction of the national debt. Let the taxes be shuffled and reshuffled any way any person may want it done; we will still come up with a budget requiring $4J billion a year if we are to maintain the standard of living that we are now maintaining and that the country wants us to maintain. To me that is absolutely logical in reasoning, and I believe it is the policy that has been followed by this government.
Again, the right of the federal government to impose taxes to meet its responsibilities does not exclude the right of the provincial government to impose taxes to meet their responsibilities. But this very double taxation which would have been a tremendous burden on the people of Canada is one of the reasons the federal-provincial agreements were entered into. Today I still maintain
220	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Cardin that those agreements are by far the best way of solving an extremely complicated problem.
Again the hon. member for Three Rivers asks that there should be a provincial-federal conference so the governments might come to an agreement. I would remind the hon. member that nine of the ten provinces of Canada have already reached agreements with the federal government. Those agreements are working satisfactorily, and the provinces which have taken up agreements with the federal government do not find themselves in any way in an inferior position to that of the federal government; nor, Mr. Speaker, do they believe or think they are in any way jeopardizing their provincial autonomy. I am positive that the governments of the nine provinces of Canada that have entered into the federal-provincial relation are as keen and as anxious to maintain this autonomy as may be the premier 'of the province of Quebec. But these provinces, I maintain, consider themselves to be autonomous provinces co-operating with the federal government in solving common problems in the best interests of the people they represent.
I am truly sorry to see that the province of Quebec does not understand this. Because of what I believe to be a political war-horse, the population of Quebec is not receiving that to which it has a perfect right. Quebec is refusing grants for universities because she is afraid she may lose her ethnic entity. Yet, Mr. Speaker, it is through the universities that our young French-Canadian men and women can acquire the knowledge, the technique and the training necessary to compete in a highly competitive world. Quebec also refused to take part in the trans-Canada highway. She not only refuses millions of dollars in that respect but she is also refusing a great economic advantage. She refuses the generous offers made under section 35 of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, whereby the federal government is willing to pay the larger part by far of the cost of reconstruction of slum areas.
I have tried sincerely to understand why the province of Quebec does not take advantage of the subsidies that are offered. I could see it or I could understand it-and I would perhaps be in favour of the refusals-if this government had in any one respect made any definite attack upon the provincial autonomy. But so far the federal government has not done so, to my mind. It may be that the province of Quebec fears that the federal government may do so in the future. But I think it would be a wise policy to do what


the other provinces in Canada have done, namely to watch carefully the movements of the federal government and, at the same time, to accept the subsidies that are now being given out to the other provinces. In other words, it would be far better for the province of Quebec to wait until the bear exists before they start shooting, and not to shoot at imaginary game.
There is another thing I wish to mention, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Three Rivers stated that the province of Quebec entered into confederation enthusiastically in order to maintain its ethnic entity. I fully agree with that statement. I also add that the situation has not changed in any way, and that confederation is still not only the best but the only way of maintaining the national unity of French Canadians in the province of Quebec. I believe that secession from confederation, either moral or physical, would be nothing less than suicide for the French-Canadian people.
I should also like to state that I have at heart, as have my French-Canadian colleagues, the interests of the language and the culture in which we have been raised. We have these interests as much at heart as has the hon. member for Three Rivers, the premier of the province of Quebec or any other French Canadian. We are equally anxious to maintain our provincial autonomy. But we do not see how co-operation between the provincial governments and the federal government can in any way be considered as an attack upon provincial autonomy.
I should also like to recall, Mr. Speaker, that some years ago it was a group of representatives from the province of Quebec, sitting in this house, who not only maintained our ethnic entity but who made it known in such a way that we French Canadians can now utilize the privileges and the rights given to all Canadians. This particular achievement, Mr. Speaker, is called national unity. These French-Canadian members who sat in this house were indeed illustrious politicians and men of high calibre, but I do not hesitate to say that the representatives we have from the province of Quebec sitting here at the present time can at least safeguard what our predecessors accomplished for us in Quebec.
It seems to me we have come a long way from the days of Upper and Lower Canada and the time when there was so much racial prejudice and misunderstanding between the two great ethnic groups in our country. It seems to me that those days have gone, and I hope forever, and I find it very gratifying indeed to see so many English Canadians learning not only the

French language but learning also French culture and the French mentality. I believe this is one of the things that has made national unity. Bilingualism is becoming a very common thing in our country, and I believe it is not only adding to our national unity but it is also giving our Canadian culture a mark of distinction.
I must admit, Mr. Speaker, that when I first came to the house I looked around for any discrimination there might be against the province of Quebec. I looked for it on the side of the government and also looked for it in the three opposition parties, and I am indeed happy to tell my constituents of the province of Quebec, or of any other province, that I have not found any evidence of any serious discrimination against the province of Quebec or against any other ethnic group in Canada. On the contrary I have found in this house, which is a pretty good cross-section of the Canadian people, a good deal of good will,' understanding and sincere desire for national unity.
I can assure the province of Quebec that if this situation should ever change, if there should be any discrimination shown toward the province of Quebec, or toward any other ethnic group in this country, they can expect to hear a loud cry from this seat and many other seats in the house, because I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that there is no master race in our country but one free democratic people that we call Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, may I join with those who have spoken before me in congratulating you on your election to your high office, but at the same time I should like to express a certain regret of my own in that this house has seen fit to render you mute for this session. I had that feeling of regret, sir, when President Eisenhower addressed the House of Commons last week and when, to my delighted surprise, I was able to understand nearly everything you addressed to us in your own language. It may have been, of course, that in the kindness of your heart you spoke in particularly simple and plain French for the benefit, shall I say, of les sauvages Anglais, but I think there must have been more to it than that. I would commend to your compatriots from Quebec the superb clarity of diction and enunciation in which you clothed your remarks that day.
I suppose also that I should join with others in congratulating the government on having been re-elected, much as one would congratulate any other conjurer for a skilful piece of sleight of hand, but I am not quite
The Address-Mr. C. Cameron sure that the people of Canada are to be equally congratulated. The following four years will perhaps tell the tale.
It has occurred to me in listening to the debate in the house since it opened that any members who were sitting in this chamber twenty or more years ago must have had a feeling as the debate rolled on that the wheel had come full circle. Listening as we have been to the tales of various hon. members of the economic tribulations that have been besetting their constituents, listening to the tales of surplus grain and retracting markets, of lay-offs and unemployment, of coal mines closing down or closed down, of canned salmon piling up in the warehouses of British Columbia and log booms accumulating along the coast for lack of lumber orders, many of these veteran members who sat here in the dark days of the thirties must have had the sensation that this was where they came in.
But, unfortunately, we cannot get up and leave the theatre of the world as we would the local movie house when the picture on the screen becomes painfully familiar. Along with the dove of peace there have been many other birds coming home to roost, birds of ill omen, and of course our government, with true ministerial nonchalance, has adopted a policy of "do not let us look now; perhaps they will fly away again."
The Conservative opposition, on the other hand, has come rushing up gun in hand to shoot the birds or frighten them away; but unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the gun in the hands of the Conservative opposition is the same old blunderbuss which proved so ineffective in the hands of the late Viscount Bennett. In fact when I read the amendment proferred by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) to the main motion, it occurred to me that there was a certain, shall I say, ambivalence in the Conservative approach to the twentieth century; for, on the one hand, this amendment bases itself firmly upon the virtues of competition, indeed of free competition no less, and then it proceeds to urge upon the government the adoption of policies that will lead to a high level of international trade, a goal which, of course, can only be reached in this modern age by the path of co-operation, the very antithesis of competition. While I am on the subject of this strange ambivalence of the Conservative party, I have been interested to note that the chief concern of their members in this house has been that struggling little corporation, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which apparently has been done dirt by the government.
One of the Conservative members the other day attempted, shall I say, to equate his
222	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. C. Cameron leader's faith in competition with modern concepts of co-operation and social responsibility, and in doing so he again revealed the state of mind of the Conservative party, and I think revealed the fact that the great Conservative party today is suffering from a bad case of schizophrenia.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we are faced again today with the same old problems which we have been enabled to ignore for the last fifteen years because of the grim cycle of events which culminated in the death of forty million human beings. There is, I think, a general admission on all sides that the means by which we came out of the dark days of the depression were closely related to the massive expenditures which it was necessary to make on war preparations in Canada.
I have been interested, of course, in the pronouncement by high political authorities that there is no danger of a recurrence of the depression in Canada. But I have also been interested to note that even the most vociferous advocates of that point of view always toss in, as a little cheering postscript, the fact that world conditions are so unsettled that we must expect a high level of military expenditure in the future.
We are told, of course, that our prosperity at the present time has resulted from the high level of investment that has taken place, and particularly investment from across the line. I have been interested in that argument, because it has seemed to me to be somewhat full of flaws. I took the trouble to investigate in the Canada Year Book the amount of foreign investments in Canada, or the increase in those investments between 1946 and 1951, as compared with defence expenditures made during the same period.
I have found that United States investments in Canada increased between 1946 and 1951 to the extent of two and a quarter billion dollars; which, of course, is a vast sum of money, and represents an enormous capital investment in the development of Canada. But it pales into insignificance when we compare it with expenditures of nearly seven and a half billion dollars upon war rehabilitation and defence expenditures during those years.
I have never been able to understand how today responsible people will try to tell us that there is no relationship whatever between these massive expenditures on military preparations and the buoyant economic conditions we have been enjoying. Nor has anyone as yet explained to me how we can hope to escape a recurrence of the conditions of the thirties, when no single fundamental economic arrangement has been altered since those dark days. The only significant change has been in the size of the public investment 

and expenditures during the years since 1939 with, of course, a consequent increase in the volume of private investment.
Apart from that, nothing has been changed. And I submit to you, sir, that an economy which is based upon continuing vast expenditure on the admittedly dangerous project of military preparation is one that is on an extremely slippery slope. Moreover I think it should be pointed out that even in this period of extreme prosperity, over which the ministerial benches wax so eloquent, there are a number of people in Canada who have been living at what can only be described as substandard levels.
In the census figures for 1951 it is revealed that 83'4 per cent of all wage earners in Canada were in receipt at that time of less than $3,000 a year, and that 83-4 per cent consisted of no less than 3,415,000 wage earners in Canada. Moreover, 2,187,000 wage earners in this country received less than $2,000 a year.
I submit to you, sir, that members of this house would do well to contemplate such figures with all due gravity. For these are the bulk of our Canadian fellow citizens; the vast majority of our fellow Canadians are in this category. And it needs no crystal ball to be able to foretell what will happen to any of those wage earners if, by any chance, they find themselves out of jobs for even a short period of time.
We socialists in this corner of the house claim no ultimate wisdom. We have no foolproof blueprint for the future. Of course we have attempted to examine the world around us, and to make that examination as objectively as possible. But lacking the rose-coloured spectacles with which members of other parties contemplate the current scene, naturally the picture presented to our eyes is somewhat different. I think that in some ways this generation, sir, is extremely fortunate, in spite of the dark days through which we have gone, in spite of the miseries and tragedies which have beset the last twenty years. We are fortunate in this regard that, perhaps uniquely in human history, we have been given a second chance. We have been given another opportunity to grapple with the problems that we have been ignoring for the last fifteen years.
At the close of the first world war we had a world ripe for radical and far-reaching changes. Nineteenth century industrial development had created problems of markets so acute that, finally, those problems culminated in the savage competition which led eventually of course to disastrous international war. And unfortunately the victors in that war reimposed the patterns of the past.

I am not going to recite all the dreary history of the inter-war period; it is well known to all of us. The dreary picture of that time was illuminated only very faintly by lights such as the Dawes plan and Locarno, finally culminating in the wreck of democracy in Germany, the wreck of the Weimar republic-, the rise of fascism and, in our own country, the crash of 1929.
I say we are fortunate, not only because we are given a second chance, as very few civilizations of the past have been; but we are fortunate also in that our society has been placed, shall I say, almost in a laboratory, and we have been subjected to laboratory experiments on our sociological organization. We have had in the last twenty years-and all of us are familiar with it-a most extraordinary history. We have had a history of a vast country, a country rich in natural resources, unable to cope with its own problems, unable to develop its resources, unable to supply the needs of its people until international feuds came to the rescue of a dying economy.
Then we had the most extraordinary transformation, almost overnight. I suggest it would do us no harm to remember that transformation and the means by which it took place. I would take your mind back, sir, to those years when, right here in the city of Ottawa, the government and parliament of that day was besieged by almost hopeless young men. I would take your mind back, sir, to the period when we had riots throughout the Dominion of Canada; and then I would ask you to turn your eyes to the events that took place immediately after or shortly before the outbreak of war in 1939 when, suddenly, all the problems with which governments had been confronted for the previous ten years vanished overnight, and almost their exact opposite took their place. Governments which had been bedevilled with problems of unemployment, bedevilled with the problem of relieving destitution, suddenly found themselves confronted with the problem of finding enough hands, enough men to do the work that required to be done.
How was it done? It was done, sir, I submit by the suspension of capitalism for the duration of the war. All the important features of the capitalist economy were put on ice. No longer did we have free competition; no longer was it possible for industrialists in Canada to produce whatever they desired; no longer was it possible for Canadian citizens to export and import to their hearts content; no longer were the productive capacities left to the hazards of individual enterprise. In its place we had goals of production set for us, quite rightly, by the government of the day. We had import and export regulations. We
The Address-Mr. C. Cameron had-and this is perhaps one of the most important features of the measures taken in these years-almost the suspension for the time being of the major factor of the capitalist economy.
I am not suggesting for one moment that there were no war profits made; there were, and scandalous war profits, for which the present government may well hang its head in shame. But I do point out, sir, that the exigencies of the war situation required that our government suspend the enjoyment of those profits for the duration of the war. This was of course accomplished by the vast war loans which were floated at the time, and which impounded for the time being that vast flood of purchasing power which was let loose on the country.
In the process a most extraordinary thing took place. Instead of a poverty-stricken, desperate people, we suddenly turned almost overnight into a people enjoying levels of prosperity hitherto unknown in our history.
I suggest to you, sir, that the history of that period is something that we would do well here to turn our eyes to. Remember how we came out of our troubles at that time, and ask ourselves if there are not some lessons to be learned in connection with the present evils which are now beginning to appear on the horizon.
Just what is our government doing, beyond denying the possibility of troubles ahead, to cope with the situation that has been presented to us in this house by hon. members from coast to coast, and which was presented the other day to a cabinet committee in this building? Just what is our government doing in regard to that situation? What is it doing with regard to the fact that the vast majority of our fellow Canadian citizens, even in times of prosperity, are living at levels that you and I would consider to be substandard, sir?
Well, they have done some extraordinary things. Last year we had the most extraordinary action, perhaps, on the part of any government, when it barefacedly came to the rescue-I should not say "rescue"-when it barefacedly, shall I say, handed out to a privileged group in this country, the fortunate owners of shares in Canadian corporations, very valuable privileges under the Income Tax Act.
What else has it done? It sold a very valuable business in 1949, which cost the taxpayers of Canada some $25 million. It sold that business to private interests for a total of $3,760,745. That has been one of this government's contributions to the economic problems of today. I would remind you, sir,

The Address-Mr. C. Cameron
that that plant, which was sold in this lighthearted manner for a small fraction of the cost to the taxpayers of Canada, was the property of these men and women who are living on incomes of $3,000, $2,000 and $1,500 a year. I suggest that all hon. members should bear that in mind.
There are rumours, of course, that further moves in this direction are about to be made. This afternoon I was interested when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), in reply to a question from one of my colleagues, stated that there was no intention on the part of the government to dispose of the Polymer Corporation. I was delighted to hear the minister make that statement because I had been greatly disturbed, sir, on reading a statement in the Financial Times no later than October 30 of this year, to this effect:
Mr. Howe announced some days ago that the government would sell the big synthetic rubber manufacturing plant located at Sarnia to private interests.
I presume that we can now expect a categorical denial of that fact from the Financial Times.

I should like to pass, sir, to another aspect of government policy that is closely linked with our domestic prosperity, namely the history of our international relations; because I think all of us today recognize that the prosperity of Canada depends in large measure upon the relationships that we cao establish with the other peoples of the world. I am going to suggest to you, sir, that our government has been even less successful in its handling of those international problems than it has been in its handling of domestic problems.
I am not going to recite all the details of the way in which Canada has acquiesced time and again in policies which have proven to be disastrous in the end. There is an old European proverb with which I have no doubt you are familiar, sir, and which translated says that he who says "A" must say "B". I would submit that our government has said not only A, it has said B and it is now halfway down the alphabet. It is true enough that now and again after the event we have a show of opposition or some protest from the government of Canada, but there are some questions that are going to be settled in the near future-they may have been settled already for all I know-whose settlement has not been made known to the people of Canada.

There is the vexed problem of the rearming of Germany. In that regard I should like to suggest to you that there has been perhaps altogether too much jubilation in certain quarters in Canada and the United States over the turn of political events in Western Germany. There are some rather fragrant flowers to be plucked from the Bonn regime. There is, for instance, Dr. Heinrich Lohse, who was reich commissar for Russian-occupied territories and in charge, under the notorious Alfred Rosenberg, of the cremation of Jews. He is now living in retirement on a pension granted him by the good Bonn administration.
Then there is Herr von Grunherr who was in charge of Jewish deportations from Norway and Denmark and who has since been appointed ambassador at Athens for Dr. Adenauer. Then there is Dr. Gerhart Peters, manager of the I. G. Farben industry affiliate which supplied the zyklon gas for the extermination of the Jews. Then of course there is the unspeakable Alfred Krupp von Bohlen, now restored to the enjoyment of his properties. I suggest to you that any intention of rearming Western Germany under this extremely dubious regime is one fraught with danger. I believe that the people of Canada and hon. members of this house are entitled to some assurance from our government that they are making representations in that regard.
I cannot help contrasting these people whom I have mentioned with another German of a very different character, the late lamented Ernst Reuter, the heroic burgomaster of West Berlin, who stood as a solid rock against the onslaught of totalitarian communism. I would remind the members of this house that Ernst Reuter was a lifelong socialist. It has been the socialists of Germany who have stood against nazi totalitarianism, on the one hand, and Soviet totalitarianism, on the other. It would be well for hon. members of this house who on occasion see fit to make sneering comments about the socialists and socialism to remember such heroic figures as the late Ernst Reuter.
I ask hon. members to examine these facts of history and to realize that before the end of this twenty-second parliament we are going to have some extremely grim and difficult tasks to perform. As I said earlier, we
The Address-Mr. C. Cameron socialists do not pretend to have all the answers. All we ask is that you look at the facts objectively, examine all the ideas that may be presented for coping with those facts, and cast aside prejudice and decide in the best interests of the people of Canada.
I do not think I can do better than to quote that great English scientist and philosopher, Bertrand (Earl) Russell, who in a recent article in an American periodical had this to say:
If, however, the reign of fear can somehow be ended "our grandchildren may look back to our time as the last moment of the dark ages from which, as from a long tunnel, mankind will have emerged into the sunshine and happiness of mutual harmony."
I submit that we shall not emerge from that dark tunnel by turning our face on the lessons of history and marching briskly back into the tunnel. I submit that it is time for all men and women of good will in Canada to sit down and study the serious problems that are going to face us and to accept ideas for their solution without prejudice, and then decide only in the interests of the people of this dominion.
